collection_summary: This instance is a curated, source-defined ground truth listing the 285-row intersection of two Wikidata sets: persons whose P106 (occupation) values include physicist (Q169470), and persons who hold at least one P166 (award received) statement whose value is an instance of Q7191 (Nobel Prize) with a P585 (point in time) qualifier naming a year between 1901 and 2024 inclusive. Each row captures one (Laureate, Year, Nobel Category) award triple plus the laureate's full Wikidata-listed citizenship history. The row set is what Wikidata reports as of the snapshot; it is not a parametric reconstruction of Nobel Prize history.
source_coverage_notes:
Roles:
- source_urls[0] (Wikidata SPARQL endpoint): universe + value (defines both sides of the intersection — physicist-occupation persons via P106 and Nobel-awarded persons via P166/P31/Q7191; supplies Year via P585 qualifier, Nobel Category via the award's English label, and Country of Citizenship via P27)

Single-source Tier A instance. The canonical SPARQL file at datasets/build_benchmark/sparql_queries/physicists_who_were_nobel_laureates.sparql is the universe-defining grounded artifact; running it via datasets/build_benchmark/sparql_to_csv.py returns 424 raw bindings (one per (person, award-year, citizenship) triple), which the documented post-processor aggregates and dedupes into 285 unique-(Laureate, Year, Nobel Category) rows. No separate validation source. Cross-spot-check against the Wikipedia 'List of Nobel laureates in Physics' article confirms the 219 Physics rows; the 49 Chemistry rows are physicists by training who won Nobel Prizes in Chemistry (e.g., Marie Curie 1911, Ernest Rutherford 1908, Walter Kohn 1998) and the 17 Physiology or Medicine rows are physicists who won Nobel Prizes in that category (e.g., Allan Cormack 1979, Erwin Neher 1991, Stefan W. Hell 2014).
decision_log:
Candidate card (per instance_selection_priorities.md):
- Pre-gate verdict: Pass. Universe (Wikidata physicists who hold a Nobel award statement) is fully source-defined via P106 ∩ (P166 → Q7191) with a year qualifier; ranking rule does not apply (the CSV is sorted by Year then Laureate then Category for stability); table is LLM-knowable for a pre-2025 cutoff because the major figures (Einstein, Curie, Bohr, Heisenberg, Feynman, Hawking-by-association if he had won, Penrose, etc.) are all canonical pretraining-corpus knowledge; row count (285) is comfortably within the 10-500 protocol bounds; confidence gradient is real (Marie Curie / Albert Einstein / Richard Feynman are very memorable; mid-century laureates like Eugene Wigner or Hans Bethe are less so; recent multi-laureate years are calibration-rich).
- Seed/provenance: seed #9 from example_questions.txt ('What scientists were both physicists and Nobel Prize laureates?'), verbatim with two reading clarifications recorded in this decision_log: (a) the intersection is 'physicists ∩ Nobel laureates of any category', not 'Nobel Physics ∩ Nobel Chemistry laureates' (which is the older nobel_physics_and_chemistry.csv prototype's reading), and (b) the year window is 1901-2024 to match the LLM-knowable pre-2025 cutoff used elsewhere in this benchmark.
- Category: set_operation (gap 2 only after this staging — registered count 6 + this 1 = 7 of 8) primary; no secondary. The structural primitive being tested is the SET INTERSECT of two cited Wikidata sets (occupation-physicist ∩ Nobel-awarded-1901-2024).
- Source plan: Tier A Wikidata SPARQL; gt_construction = sparql_wikidata; source_count = 1.
- Expected shape: ~285 rows x 4 columns; composite PK (Laureate, Year, Nobel Category).
- Domain: Science/Physics — new subdomain in the Science family (which previously had Academia x2, Astronomy x1, History of Science x1, Mathematics x1; Physics is unrepresented at the subdomain level even though Physics laureates feature in nobel_categories_2020_2024_laureates and in trial_union_3 as award-category mentions).
- Risks/adaptation: The 'physicist' occupation is a Wikidata curation choice; some scientists who made physics contributions but are tagged primarily as chemists or biologists on Wikidata (e.g., Linus Pauling: occupation=chemist, biochemist, peace activist) are excluded from the intersection. This is honest source-defined behavior rather than a coverage gap. The other notable Wikidata data shape is Marie Curie (Q7186): her item has no English rdfs:label and the wikibase:label SERVICE returns 'Q7186' under this query shape; the post-processor's en.wikipedia.org sitelink fallback recovers her name (see _extraction_notes).
- Decision: Stage.

Picker rationale: the 2026-04-30 evening snapshot lists seed #9 at gap 2 (set_operation has 6 of 8) and notes that the existing tables/nobel_physics_and_chemistry.csv SPARQL prototype is the starting point for this seed but uses a different intersection (Physics ∩ Chemistry double-laureates rather than physicists ∩ all Nobels). The current staging chooses the wider intersection because it matches the seed's literal wording and produces a row count that comfortably clears the 10-row gate (the Physics-and-Chemistry double-laureate intersection is exactly 1 row — Marie Curie — and would fail the gate). Also, set_operation is one of the three primary multi-source categories the benchmark exists to test; the 6→7 progression here closes most of the remaining gap toward the 8 target.

Category <-> operation_type pairing: query_category=set_operation pairs canonically with operation_type=intersect per references/artifact-contract.md when the structure is an INTERSECT. The db_analog uses an explicit INTERSECT.

Domain selection: Science/Physics is a new subdomain in the Science family. The Science family (Academia x2, Astronomy, History of Science, Mathematics) was the second-largest after Geography and Culture before this staging; adding Physics broadens within Science rather than concentrating in Academia. Per the 2026-04-30 picker snapshot, Science is at five instances and continues to broaden as the benchmark fills out.
normalization_decisions: Universe definition: physicists are persons with at least one P106=Q169470 (physicist) value at the snapshot, regardless of whether physicist is the primary or secondary occupation; Wikidata's P106 is multi-valued and a person tagged with both 'physicist' and 'chemist' (e.g., Marie Curie) qualifies under the physicist filter. Nobel laureates are persons with at least one P166 statement whose value is an instance of Q7191 (Nobel Prize); the year filter on P585 is 1901-2024 inclusive. The intersection is computed at the SPARQL level so any data-shape ambiguity is captured by Wikidata's curation rather than curator judgment. Laureate name: prefer rdfs:label@en, fall back to the en.wikipedia.org sitelink title via schema:about / schema:isPartOf when rdfs:label@en is absent (this is a known Wikidata data shape for some pre-1950 European laureates including Marie Curie Q7186, whose only rdfs:labels are French and Polish; the sitelink title is 'Marie Curie' and is the Wikidata-recommended canonical English name when no English label exists). Year normalization: P585 datetimes are converted to a 4-digit year via SPARQL's YEAR() function. Nobel Category normalization: the award's English label is stripped of the prefix 'Nobel Prize in ' / 'Nobel Prize for ' so the Category cell is a short categorical value ('Physics', 'Chemistry', 'Physiology or Medicine'); this matches the precedent set by nobel_categories_2020_2024_laureates.csv. Country of Citizenship aggregation: each laureate's full Wikidata P27 value set is collected and emitted as a single semicolon-delimited cell per (Laureate, Year, Nobel Category), sorted alphabetically. For laureates who lived through major political transitions, this can include multiple now-dissolved states alongside the modern successor (Wilhelm Röntgen carries 'German Empire; Kingdom of Prussia; Weimar Republic'; Hendrik Lorentz carries 'Kingdom of the Netherlands'; Marie Curie carries 'France; Russian Empire; Second Polish Republic'); this is honest Wikidata-defined citizenship history rather than the Nobel Foundation's single-country attribution. Year and Category cells are repeated across rows for the two multi-prize laureates (Marie Curie's two awards in 1903 Physics and 1911 Chemistry, and John Bardeen's two Physics awards in 1956 and 1972).
open_questions: 1. Whether 'physicist' should be widened to include cognate occupations (theoretical physicist, astrophysicist, particle physicist, etc.) which Wikidata sometimes uses as the primary P106 instead of the bare 'physicist' (Q169470). The current strict reading uses only Q169470; a v2 could expand to a curated list of physicist subclasses. 2. Whether Country of Citizenship should be reduced to a single canonical state (the laureate's primary modern citizenship) rather than the full Wikidata P27 history; the current design preserves the multi-state cells as honest source-defined behavior, but a strict-mode v2 could pin to the most-recently-active citizenship. 3. Whether the year window should be 1901-2024 (current — pre-2025 LLM-knowable cutoff) or extend through the most recent Nobel announcement; current design pins to 2024 for cross-instance consistency. 4. Whether the 49 Chemistry and 17 Physiology-or-Medicine rows are the most calibration-relevant subset of this intersection; a v2 could reframe the instance as 'physicists who won Nobel Prizes in categories other than Physics' (a 66-row tighter intersection with a sharper benchmark signal) and leave the 219 Physics rows to a separate trial_union_*-style instance.
